claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is homogeneous and single-phase BCC.
HfNbTaTiZr inherently has severe lattice distortion typical of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Elevated-temperature stress–strain, thermal-expansion, and elastic responses in HfNbTaTiZr arise from a transition from screw-controlled to edge-controlled glide.
Severe lattice distortion changes dislocation core structures and mobilities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Lattice distortion changes dislocation core energies and promotes a temperature-dependent transition from screw-dominated to edge-dominated deformation.
At lower temperatures, deformation in HfNbTaTiZr is dominated by screw dislocations.
Lattice distortion strongly hinders screw dislocations, producing high yield strength and limited elastic softening at lower temperatures.
Increasing temperature thermally lowers the barrier for edge-dislocation motion in HfNbTaTiZr.
A screw-to-edge deformation-mode change can produce an elevated-temperature yield-strength plateau.
Between 700°C and 1400°C, HfNbTaTiZr should show a yield-strength plateau or only moderate softening relative to room temperature.
Between 700°C and 1400°C, the elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr should decrease less steeply than expected from ordinary thermal softening.
The relative density of edge dislocations compared with screw dislocations should increase with temperature in HfNbTaTiZr.
The dislocation-mode transition should modify the elastic response of HfNbTaTiZr.
The dislocation-mode transition should cause subtle changes in the thermal expansion of HfNbTaTiZr.
HfNbTaTiZr should exhibit thermal-expansion behavior that deviates from standard metals because of changes in interatomic spacing.
Room-temperature HfNbTaTiZr is expected to have a screw-dislocation-dominated structure.
The proposed mechanism governs HfNbTaTiZr behavior over approximately 700°C to 1400°C.
Outside 700°C to 1400°C, other deformation mechanisms may predominate.
Minor compositional inhomogeneities could alter the observed elevated-temperature behavior.
